newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand considers floating domestic sugar prices.
newsitem.headline: Thailand considers floating domestic sugar prices.

text.p: Thailand is considering floating its local sugar prices to avoid possible shortages caused by millers smuggling out sugar to sell in a more lucrative world market, Thai Cane and Sugar Board secretary general Pramote Vidtayasuk said on Monday.
Pramote told Reuters that the board was considering the issue and may either completely float or launch a managed float of the local prices by next year.
Thailand has pegged local sugar prices at 12.00 baht a kg ($0.39) for white sugar and 13.00 baht for refined sugar since 1981.
The sugar industry is managed by the Thai Cane and Sugar Board which is controlled by the government, millers and sugar cane farmers.

Each year, the board will set up a quota for three types of sugar -- the white-only quota A for domestic consumption, the raw-only quota B for export by the Thai Cane and Sugar Corp and quota C comprising both white and raw to be exported by private sector.
Sugar production for the 1996/97 crushing season (Nov-June) was fixed at around 1.67 million tonnes for quota A, 800,000 tonnes for quota B and 3.4 million tonnes for quota C.
Pramote said floating local sugar prices would depend a lot on the baht and the world white sugar prices.

"If the baht remains at current levels of around 31 per dollar and white sugar prices stay this high, the board will have to do something to narrow the gap between local and world prices or producers will be tempted to export," he said.
"We are looking at a level around 15.00 baht a kg which should be fair to producers and it will encourage people to sell more to the local market," he added.
October white surged $4.30 in London on Friday to close at $328.50 per tonne.
Pramote was vague on details of the flotation, and declined to elaborate whether the board planned to liberalise quota A sugar by scrapping the quota itself as well as freeing the price ceiling.
"The proposal is at a very early stage. The sugar industry is very sensitive and we have to be careful before making any policy change," Pramote said.
